passage: Transcript: Let's look at printmaking — the art of making multiple impressions of an image from a prepared surface. The crucial thing to understand is that different techniques put the ink in different places, and that changes how the print looks. Start with the oldest method, the woodcut. The artist carves away the parts that should stay white, leaving the design standing up in relief; ink sits on the raised surface, and the carved-away areas print as blank paper. So in a relief print, the lines you see are the parts left uncut. Now contrast engraving and etching, which work the opposite way. These are intaglio methods — the word comes from the Italian for 'to cut in.' The artist cuts grooves into a metal plate; ink is pushed down into those grooves, the flat surface is wiped clean, and damp paper is pressed hard enough to pull the ink up out of the lines. So in intaglio the ink comes from below the surface, not on top of it. One more, invented around 1800: lithography, which uses no carving at all. It relies on a simple chemical fact — that grease and water repel each other. The artist draws with a greasy crayon on a flat stone; the drawn areas hold ink and the wet blank areas reject it. Three logics, then: on top, cut in, or flat.

passage: Transcript: The history of photography is really a story of two problems: how to capture an image, and how to make copies of it. The first practical process was announced in France in 1839 — the daguerreotype. It produced an astonishingly sharp image directly on a silver-coated copper plate. But it had a serious limitation: each daguerreotype was a unique object. There was no negative, so you could not make a second print. If you wanted two portraits, you had to sit for the camera twice. At almost the same moment, in England, William Talbot developed a rival process using paper. His images were softer, less crisp than the daguerreotype — and at first that made them less popular. But Talbot's method had a decisive advantage: it produced a negative, from which any number of positive prints could be made. And that, in the long run, is the principle that won. The negative-to-positive idea is the basis of nearly all film photography that followed. Now jump ahead to 1888, when George Eastman put a long roll of film inside a simple box camera and sold it with a slogan: 'You press the button, we do the rest.' The customer shot a hundred pictures, mailed the whole camera back to the factory for developing, and got it returned reloaded. Photography, once the work of specialists, was suddenly something anyone could do.

passage: Transcript: Okay, let's talk about why countries trade even when one of them seems better at making everything. The intuition most people start with is called absolute advantage — if I can produce more cloth per hour than you can, I have an absolute advantage in cloth. But that's not actually what drives trade. What matters is comparative advantage, which is about opportunity cost. Here's the classic example. Suppose in one hour Portugal can make either two bottles of wine or two bolts of cloth, while England can make one bottle of wine or half a bolt of cloth. Portugal is better at both — absolute advantage in both goods. But look at what each gives up. For Portugal, making one bolt of cloth means giving up one bottle of wine. For England, making one bolt of cloth means giving up two bottles of wine. So cloth is cheaper for Portugal in terms of forgone wine. Portugal should specialize where its opportunity cost is lowest — cloth — and England should specialize in wine, and then they trade. What researchers found, going all the way back to David Ricardo in 1817, is that both countries end up with more of both goods than if each tried to make everything itself. The lesson: it's relative cost, not raw productivity, that tells you who should make what.

passage: Transcript: Let's dig into one of the most important ideas in all of economics, and it's deceptively simple: opportunity cost. The opportunity cost of any choice is the value of the next-best thing you gave up to get it. Notice — the next-best alternative, not all the alternatives added together. That distinction trips people up. Here's an example. Say you have a free evening, and your options are studying, working a shift for forty dollars, or going to a concert you'd value at, oh, sixty dollars. If you choose to study, your opportunity cost isn't a hundred dollars — it's sixty, the value of the single best thing you passed up, the concert. Now here's the part I really want you to sit with. Opportunity cost includes things that never show up on a price tag. When a company builds a factory on land it already owns, an accountant might record no cost for the land. But the economist asks: what could that land have earned if it were rented out or sold? That forgone rent is a real cost of using the land, even though no money changed hands. Economists call these implicit costs. So whenever you evaluate a decision, don't just ask what you paid — ask what you gave up. That's the true cost.

passage: Transcript: Today I want to compare two ends of a spectrum: perfect competition and monopoly. In perfect competition, you have many small firms selling an identical product — think of wheat farmers. No single farmer can influence the price; each just accepts whatever the market sets. We call such a firm a price taker. Because entry is easy, if profits are high, new firms flood in until those extra profits disappear. A monopoly is the opposite. One firm is the entire market — maybe it holds a patent, or controls a key resource, or the government granted it exclusive rights. A monopolist is a price maker: it can raise the price by choosing to sell less. But — and students often miss this — even a monopolist can't charge any price it wants. It's still limited by the demand curve; push the price too high and customers simply buy less or go without. Now, why do we care? The concern with monopoly isn't just high prices. It's that the monopolist produces less than a competitive market would, and that reduction — output that never gets made even though buyers would value it — is what economists call deadweight loss. Society loses those transactions. That inefficiency, more than the profits themselves, is the reason antitrust law exists.

passage: Transcript: Let's clear up two numbers you hear on the news constantly: GDP and the unemployment rate. GDP — gross domestic product — is the market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a year. Two words there matter a lot. Final — we count the loaf of bread, not separately the flour and the wheat that went into it, or we'd be double-counting. And within a country — it's about where production happens, not who owns the company. Now, unemployment. Here's what surprises people: to be counted as unemployed, you must be without a job and actively looking for one. Someone who's given up searching — a discouraged worker — isn't counted as unemployed at all; they've left the labor force. That's why the official rate can actually fall in a bad economy, if enough frustrated people simply stop looking. The two numbers relate through something called Okun's law, a rough rule of thumb: when output grows faster than usual, unemployment tends to drop, and when the economy shrinks, unemployment climbs. It's not a precise formula — it's an observed regularity. But it captures the basic link: producing more stuff generally means putting more people to work.

passage: Transcript: Traditional economics assumes people are rational — that we weigh costs and benefits and choose what's best for us. Behavioral economics asks: what if we don't? And it turns out, in predictable ways, we don't. Take loss aversion. Experiments show that the pain of losing twenty dollars feels roughly twice as strong as the pleasure of gaining twenty dollars. The amounts are identical, but our reactions aren't. That asymmetry explains why people hold onto losing investments far too long — selling would make the loss feel real. Here's another one, the anchoring effect. If I ask you whether the population of a city is more or less than ten million, and then ask you to guess the actual number, your guess will land higher than if I'd first said one million. The initial figure anchors you, even when it's arbitrary and you know it's arbitrary. Now, the point of all this isn't that people are stupid. It's that these biases are systematic — they push in a consistent direction, so we can anticipate them. And that's powerful. If a government wants more people to save for retirement, it can simply make enrollment the default and let inertia work in savers' favor. That's a nudge — same choices available, just a smarter starting point.

passage: Transcript: A central bank — the Federal Reserve in the U.S., the Bank of Korea here — is not a regular bank; you and I can't open an account there. Its customers are commercial banks and the government. Its main job is monetary policy: managing the supply of money and credit to keep the economy stable. The primary tool is the interest rate. When the central bank lowers its key rate, borrowing gets cheaper throughout the economy, businesses and households borrow and spend more, and activity picks up. When it raises the rate, borrowing costs climb, spending cools, and — this is usually the goal — inflation comes down. So there's a balancing act. Cut rates too much and you risk overheating and rising prices; raise them too much and you can choke off growth and cause a recession. Notice the tension there: the same tool that fights inflation can also trigger unemployment. That's why these decisions are so hard. One more crucial point: most central banks are deliberately kept independent from the elected government. Why? Because a politician facing an election is tempted to juice the economy with cheap money right now and let inflation become someone else's problem later. Independence is meant to protect the currency from that short-term temptation.

passage: Transcript: Let's talk about how we classify taxes, because the vocabulary matters for every policy debate you'll ever hear. The key distinction is progressive versus regressive. A progressive tax takes a larger percentage from higher incomes — most income taxes work this way, with rates that rise as you earn more. A regressive tax does the opposite: it takes a larger percentage from lower incomes. Now, that sounds strange — who designs a tax to hit the poor harder? But watch. A sales tax has a single flat rate, say ten percent, applied to everyone equally. Sounds fair. But a lower-income family spends nearly all of what it earns, so almost all its income gets taxed, while a wealthy family saves a big chunk that's never touched by the sales tax. So a flat rate ends up regressive in effect, even though the rate itself is identical for everyone. That gap between the stated rate and the real burden is exactly what economists watch for. One more term: the tax base — that's what's being taxed, whether income, purchases, or property. A good rule policymakers follow is to keep rates moderate but the base broad, because very high rates on a narrow base give people a strong incentive to avoid or evade the tax.
